blogs.title: Lima v2.3: Native on Windows, VMnet on Linux, and menu TUI
blogs.content: Posted on November 8, 2026 by audra Back in July with v2.2 , we added support for Windows guests. On November 6, we shipped v2.3 of Lima and now it runs without extra dependencies on Windows: VMs start through the same Host Compute System that powers WSL2, without QEMU and without a Unix toolchain. On Linux, VMs are getting the “ real IP address” networking that Mac users have had through ` socket_vmnet `. And on every host, managing your VMs gets friendlier with a new terminal UI . What is Lima? Lima (Linux Machines) is a command-line tool to launch local virtual machines. Originally focused on running containers on a laptop and promoting containerd to Mac users, Lima joined the CNCF as a Sandbox project in September 2022 and was promoted to Incubating in October 2025. Today, Lima supports a wide variety of non-container workloads, non-macOS hosts, non-Linux guests and robust AI sandboxing. If you are using Homebrew, Lima can be installed using: brew install lima If you are on Windows, Lima can be installed through PowerShell using: winget install Lima.Lima For other installation methods, see https://lima-vm.io/docs/installation/ . Updates in v2.3 Windows hosts: the HCS driver (experimental) Until now, Windows users who wanted Lima had two options: the ` wsl2 ` or QEMU driver. v2.3 adds a third, the new ` hcs ` driver . It talks directly to the Windows Host Compute System (HCS) API, the Windows virtualization layer that WSL2 is built on. In the v2.2 announcement, we said that our LFX mentorship would “explore and evaluate native virtualization support for Windows hosts”. A few weeks later, that research has become a working driver. Before you try it Enable virtualization on your machine. Add yourself to the ` Hyper-V Administrators ` group from an Administrator PowerShell, then restart your terminal: net localgroup "Hyper-V Administrators" <user name> /add Then run Lima from a shell: limactl start --vm-type hcs --plain --dns 8.8.8.8 lima Current limitations Only `plain` mode is supported. There are no file mounts and no dynamic port forwarding yet. Only one HCS instance can run at a time, because the HCN network subnet is fixed. A DNS server must be specified explicitly using the `–dns` flag. See the HCS driver docs for details. More Windows improvements Lima now recognizes Windows built-in SSH client, handles Windows paths correctly, and uses a matching mount server. ` limactl shell` , ` limactl copy `, and reverse-sshfs mounts work on a stock Windows install. If you install QEMU in its default location, Lima previously could not find it until you added ` %PROGRAMFILES%\QEMU ` to your ` PATH ` by hand. Lima now checks these common install directories automatically. The Windows guests introduced in v2.2 could boot, but you could not customize them at startup. They now have limited support for ` provision `. ` system `, ` user `, ` data ` and ` dependency ` scripts let you install software and configure the guest automatically. ` boot `, ` yq ` and `ansible` modes are not supported yet. See the Windows guest docs for details. Linux hosts: Real networking for VMs On macOS, ` socket_vmnet ` gives VMs an IP address that the host can reach directly. Linux had no equivalent, so the ` lima: shared `, ` lima: host ` and ` lima: bridged ` networks only worked on macOS. v2.3 introduces ` lima-privileged-net `, a small privileged helper for Linux hosts which: creates a Linux bridge for each network and assigns the gateway address, runs ` dnsmasq ` for DHCP and DNS, and adds NAT and forwarding rules for ` shared ` mode, creates one tap device per instance, gives it to the calling user, and attaches it to the bridge, removes the network again when the last instance leaves, and only ever touches interfaces that follow Lima’s naming scheme. One-time setup on Linux: the `sudoers` file Creating bridges and tap devices requires root, so there are two steps before your first start: Install Lima as root, and install ` dnsmasq `. ` limactl sudoers ` refuses to generate rules for a helper that isn’t root-owned. Generate and install the rules: limactl sudoers >etc_sudoers.d_lima less etc_sudoers.d_lima sudo install -o root -m 0440 etc_sudoers.d_lima /etc/sudoers.d/lima rm etc_sudoers.d_lima Then start an instance on a managed network: limactl start --network=lima:shared --vm-type=qemu See the Linux networking docs for details. macOS hosts: Give your VM a real disk With v2.3, Lima can now attach a block device (USB drive or an external SSD) to VZ guests, without going through a file share. In order for this feature to work, sudo privileges are required to configure it. One-time setup on macOS: the `sudoers` file Opening a host disk requires root, so there are two steps before your first `–block-device` start: The helper and every directory above it must be root-owned. Typical Homebrew installs are user-writable, so extract the macOS release archive into ` /opt/lima ` and run ` /opt/lima/bin/limactl ` directly:As your regular user, generate the rule, review it, and install it: sudo install -d -o root -g wheel -m 0755 /opt/lima sudo tar --no-same-owner -xzf lima-VERSION-Darwin-ARCH.tar.gz -C /opt/lima 2. As your regular user, generate the rule, review it, and install it: limactl sudoers --block-device=/dev/disk4 >etc_sudoers.d_lima less etc_sudoers.d_lima visudo -cf etc_sudoers.d_lima sudo install -o root -g wheel -m 0444 etc_sudoers.d_lima /etc/sudoers.d/lima rm etc_sudoers.d_lima The rule only lets your user run the helper on that one device. When you regenerate the file, include every grant you want to keep, because installing it replaces the previous file. After these steps, then it’s a single flag: limactl start --vm-type=vz --block-device=/dev/disk4 template:default Inside the guest, each device appears under ` /dev/disk/by-id/virtio-<name> ` (for example ` virtio-disk4 `). From there you can partition, format and mount it as you like. You can repeat ` --block-device ` to attach more than one device. 💡 If you don’t have a spare drive, you can also test with a RAM disk: ` hdiutil attach -nomount ram://65536 ` ⚠️ macOS mounts external drives automatically. Unmount the drive first (e.g. ` diskutil unmountDisk /dev/disk4` , don’t eject it), or the VM fails to start with ` resource busy `. Built with security in mind Giving a VM raw access to a disk is powerful, so it needs to be safe. An earlier implementation of this feature was reverted after a security report. The version in v2.3 was redesigned around a few principles: Lima itself never opens the disk as root. A dedicated privileged helper, ` lima-privileged-block-device `, does it instead. Lima refuses to use the helper unless it and every directory above it are owned by root and not writable by regular users. Access is granted per device , through a ` sudoers ` file generated by ` limactl sudoers --block-device=/dev/diskN `. The helper only accepts real macOS disk device nodes, and only the ones listed in that file. You review the file, validate it with ` visudo -cf` , and then install it yourself. Starting a VM never grants root access silently. Instances that share a ` LIMA_HOME ’ lock the whole disk, including its raw and block aliases and partitions. This prevents two VMs from writing to the same disk. ⚠️ Never grant access to your boot or system disk. Never mount the same filesystem on the host and in a guest (or in two guests) at the same time. The full setup guide is in the disk docs . More for macOS Set ` osOpts.Darwin.suppressFirstLoginSetup: true ` and Lima pre-configures macOS guests so the first-login setup screens are skipped. This is useful for headless or automated VMs. ` audio.microphone: true ` gives VZ guests a capture device in addition to speakers. It is opt-in, so macOS only asks for microphone permission when you enable it. ` nestedVirtualization ` now works with the HVF accelerator on aarch64 (requires QEMU 11.1 or later and macOS 15...

blogs.title: We organized Sustainability Month. Here’s what we learned. 🌱
blogs.content: Posted on November 7, 2026 by Elif Samedin - CNCF Ambassador | Diana Todea - CNCF Ambassador, Kepler maintainer, TAG Operational Resilience Lead What do Kubernetes resource allocation, eBPF, carbon observability, and GPUs have in common? Quite a lot, actually. Especially when you start looking at them through the lens of environmental sustainability. This October, we brought these conversations together as part of Cloud Native Sustainability Month . And while the idea was to help our community learn more about sustainability, we ended up learning quite a few things ourselves. But first, a little backstory. How did we get here? It all started in 2023, when the CNCF TAG Environmental Sustainability launched the first Cloud Native Sustainability Week. The idea was simple: bring cloud native communities together to explore how technology can become more environmentally sustainable. What began as a week of events eventually grew into a month-long initiative, with sustainability efforts continuing under CNCF TAG Operational Resilience . Fast-forward to October 2026, and communities were once again bringing their own perspectives to the conversation. In Bucharest, we joined the initiative with a virtual meetup featuring speakers from across the cloud native ecosystem. Our goal? Make sustainability a little less abstract and a lot more relevant to the engineering decisions we make every day. So, what did we learn? 1. Sustainability is closer to our everyday work than we think. When someone mentions environmental sustainability in tech, it’s easy to think about carbon emissions, renewable energy, or data centers. But what about the resources we allocate to Kubernetes workloads? The CPU cycles we consume? Or that extra GPU we’re considering adding to our infrastructure? Our speakers approached sustainability from different angles, and that’s what made the discussions interesting. We explored carbon observability with OpenTelemetry , energy metrics, Kubernetes resource allocation, eBPF , GPU efficiency, and even how data center efficiency is calculated. Different topics, but a common thread: sometimes, making technology more sustainable starts with questioning how we use the resources we already have. And that’s something most of us can relate to. 2. You don’t need to be a sustainability expert to join the conversation. This one applies to attendees, speakers, and organizers alike. Sustainability is a big topic. There’s a lot to learn, and honestly, it can be a little intimidating when you don’t know where to start. But that’s exactly why community events matter. You don’t need to understand every aspect of carbon accounting to ask whether your workloads are using resources efficiently. And you don’t need years of experience in sustainable computing to share an experiment or ask a good question. Sometimes, a lightning talk about something you’ve been working on is enough to get others thinking. And sometimes, the most interesting conversations start with someone saying, “Have you considered trying this?” 3. Organizing is a learning experience, too. We usually think about events from the attendees’ perspective. What will they learn? Which talks will they find interesting? Will they leave with something useful? But there’s another side to it. As organizers, we get to discover projects, connect with speakers, and explore topics we might not otherwise encounter. Of course, there’s also the less glamorous part: making sure everything comes together—and yes, sometimes wondering whether anyone will actually show up. But seeing people come together around a shared interest makes the effort worthwhile. One thing we’ve come to appreciate is that you don’t need a huge conference or an elaborate program to create something valuable. A few good talks, curious people, and a topic worth discussing can go a long way. The event is over. Now what? One of the challenges with sustainability is figuring out what to do after the conversation ends. The good news? There are plenty of ways to get involved. If you’re an engineer, start by looking at how efficiently your applications use resources. Explore projects like Kepler , a CNCF incubating project, and experiment with energy metrics or share something you’ve learned. If you’re interested in open source, there are opportunities to contribute through code, documentation, testing, and community discussions. And if you’re a community organizer, why not bring sustainability into your next meetup? You don’t need to dedicate an entire event to it. Start with a lightning talk, invite someone working on an interesting project, or organize a discussion around a problem your community is already facing. Small steps count, too. See you in 2027? Looking back, organizing Sustainability Month reminded us of something we already love about the cloud native community: there’s always someone willing to share what they know, and someone else curious enough to learn. We certainly don’t have all the answers about making cloud native technology more sustainable. But we have a community that’s willing to ask questions, experiment, and figure things out together. And that’s a pretty good place to start. So, if you’re part of a cloud native community and have been thinking about organizing something for Sustainability Month 2027, consider this your invitation. Bring your ideas, your questions, and your community. We’ll figure out the rest together. 🌱 Share
